idiom_name: language ownership and borrows; Box / Rc / Arc / Weak from std
implementation_notes: Rust generalises the pattern into the language: every value has exactly one owner, moves transfer ownership statically, and borrows are non-owning, so use-after-free is rejected at compile time before any smart pointer is involved. The standard handles select the ownership model - Box<T> for a unique heap allocation, Rc<T> for shared ownership within one thread, Arc<T> for the thread-safe atomic variant, and Weak<T> (from Rc/Arc) for non-owning edges that must be upgraded with upgrade() and checked - while Deref gives them pointer behaviour through auto-deref and Drop gives deterministic release at scope exit. Custom smart pointers are written by implementing Deref and Drop; RefCell/Cell add interior mutability where the borrow checker cannot express the sharing.
pitfalls: Rc<T> is neither Send nor Sync: sharing across threads needs Arc<T>, and holding an Rc<RefCell<T>> across an .await point will not compile in Send futures.
Reference cycles built from Rc/Arc leak - Rust's sharing is refcounting - so break them with Weak exactly as with shared_ptr/weak_ptr, and remember Drop never runs for a leaked cycle.
Weak::upgrade races with the last owner dropping and returns None; the compiler will not remind you to handle that case.
unsafe raw pointers and mem::forget bypass the ownership model; reaching for them to imitate a C++ design reintroduces exactly the bugs the language removes.
